prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock based on the magic-wavelength condition and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I change my preferred configuration from B043 to B006. In round 1 I kept IceCube first but said I held it with less certainty, and the exchange has settled that for me. The discovery I value most is B043, but a prize has to be one I can put names on. Halzen drove IceCube and AMANDA, Spiering is a founding figure of neutrino telescopy, but DUMAND, Baikal and the wider AMANDA and IceCube leadership all have claims, and nobody in the committee, including me, can say from memory who was decisive. The chair's question about what I would need from an outside report is therefore real: it would have to show that Halzen and Spiering together, and not a larger group, carried the idea from the first detectors to the 2013 diffuse flux. Until that exists, B043 is a good discovery without a defensible credit. B006 by contrast is a complete chain from idea to measurement: Katori's magic-wavelength condition removes the lattice light shift, and Ye's group turned it into stability and accuracy at 10^-18, with gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre-sized sample. That is a quantitative clue from nature, a relativistic effect seen in a laboratory sample, and independent groups at RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB and SYRTE reproduce and compare such clocks. I accept that the clock is not yet a discovery of a new phenomenon, but the committee has repeatedly rewarded inventions that open a new regime of measurement, and this is one. The citation names the invention and its realisation, not the record alone.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 comb prize and Wineland's 2012 prize is the honest objection, and I raised it myself in my opening. I now think the magic-wavelength lattice clock, with many thousands of neutral atoms interrogated at once, is a distinct step, but a sceptic can still call it an excellent advance within a recognised line. The priority record for 2001-03 has not been checked against reports, and Ludlow, Lemonde, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups have real claims that a pair leaves out. The redefinition of the second and any fundamental-physics result (varying constants, dark matter) are still pending, so the payoff I care about most, a clue from nature, has not arrived yet. If an expert report shows that Katori's priority is weak or that the credit really belongs to a wider group, I would return to B043 or B004.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube first to optical lattice clocks, keeping B043 as an alternative, and noted possible proximity bias toward B043.
responses.response: I follow Pearce's move and I now stand where he does. His round-1 argument that quantified, reproduced performance is what an instrument builder trusts is the argument I could not answer for B043, where the claim of 'who built it' is spread over several decades and several detectors. I still think his original reading of IceCube as a new window is correct. I would ask him one thing in return: that we ask the outside report to cover Halzen, Spiering, Baikal and DUMAND anyway, so B043 stays a live alternative for a later year and not a dropped one.

responses.point: Kroll argues that optical lattice clocks have a clean lineage from concept to record performance, with every systematic traceable to a physical effect, and discloses a year in Hall's laboratory at JILA.
responses.response: Kroll's argument is the one that moved me, together with Lindroth's. I agree that traceable systematics and several independent laboratories are what tell a durable result from a fashionable one. I would not call it a discovery in the sense of a new phenomenon, as I said in round 1, and Kroll himself concedes the redefinition of the second is still ahead. On his disclosure, a year in Hall's laboratory during a PhD, with no collaboration with Katori or Ye, does not seem to me a reason for recusal. I would ask him to say so openly in the vote record and let the chair confirm that the committee is content.

responses.point: Lindroth wants the B006 citation to name the invention and its realisation, and admits she has not settled how to weigh Katori's idea against the performance records from Ye's group.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and I think that is the right place to put the weight. The citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its realisation at 10^-18, so that Katori's concept and Ye's demonstration of accuracy, stability and the redshift measurement are both visible, and no record is credited as such. As Secretary I would send the priority question on 2001-03 to outside experts before the vote, because the Katori-Ye pairing is where I would expect a challenge, and I would rather have it answered than argue it from memory.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that B004 is a genuinely new state of matter, distinct from the 2016 prize because the Z2 class is symmetry protected, and asks whether a better ruler should outrank a new state of matter.
responses.response: Eriksson's distinction from the 2016 prize is fair and I accept that Z2 topological insulators are a separate step. My difficulty remains the credit boundary. The HgTe route that Molenkamp realised was proposed by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and with Zhang deceased the committee cannot repair the gap, so a trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp stitches a theory prize to an experiment that other theorists proposed. To his question about a ruler versus a new state of matter: I do not treat these as ranked in principle, but I would support B004 as my second alternative if the credit boundary can be settled.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B009 for its prediction-to-discovery logic and the compact Bistritzer-MacDonald model, and ranks B043 only seventh because source identification is unfinished.
responses.response: I accept his attribution point on B043 without reservation, and it is the reason I am moving. I do not think that unfinished astronomy makes the discovery premature, and I would still defend the diffuse flux as the basis of any citation. On B009, I admire the model, but the pairing mechanism is open, the field is about eight years old and Yuan Cao cannot be named. I do not see maturity being resolved by this year's vote, so I keep it off my list.

responses.point: Olsson argues that B009 is the only shortlisted case where the experiment is the first of its kind and the field is still opening, and concedes the clock case is more mature and cleaner.
responses.response: I take seriously her point that a field still opening is a reason to recognise it and not to wait. My worry is that eight years is too short to know which of the moire results is the lasting core. She has conceded that B006 is the more mature and cleaner alternative, and on the question of what the committee can defend as a final public position I think that concession decides it.

uncertainties: Whether an outside expert report on 2001-03 supports Katori's priority for the magic-wavelength lattice clock and whether the Katori-Ye pair stands against the claims of Ludlow, Lemonde, Hinkley and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups.
Whether the committee accepts the optical lattice clock as an invention distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes and not as a precision refinement of them.
Whether a report on Halzen, Spiering and the Baikal, AMANDA and DUMAND precursors would let B043 stand on the diffuse flux alone in a future year.
Whether the credit boundary in B004 around Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang can be bridged within three names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent. None of the candidates in B006, B043 or B004 is connected to Uppsala, to David Gross, to Thomas Van Riet or to my other collaborators, and my own work in string theory and cosmology is not on the shortlist, so I am a non-expert on all eight. I note that I am listed as a co-opted member and Secretary, and that I handle the requests for outside reports. I see no reason for Kroll, Lindroth, Johansson or Olsson to recuse on the basis of their disclosures, but I would let the chair rule.
